Short Commentary:
The United States’ renewed push to rally allies in the defense field, the Pentagon chief telling Asian allies to raise defence spending to 5% of GDP like Europe, particularly under the Trump 2.0 administration and through Secretary Hegseth’s aggressive posture, may resonate with traditional security partners. However, when it comes to ASEAN, winning trust is a far more complicated affair. 

First, ASEAN’s Strategic DNA is Non-Alignment and Hedging. ASEAN’s foundational ethos is built on strategic autonomy, non-alignment, and regional or ASEAN centrality. Most member-states, if not almost all, except the Philippines, resist formal alliances or rigid bloc commitments. They are master practitioners of hedging, carefully balancing their ties between major powers, particularly the U.S. and China. The more Washington demands overt military alignment, the more ASEAN countries instinctively pull back. ASEAN does not want to be a chessboard for great power rivalry. It wants to be a player shaping regional rules.

Second, the U.S. often frames defense cooperation in terms of arms sales and interoperability. However, ASEAN countries prioritize capacity-building, maritime domain awareness, humanitarian assistance, disaster relief, economic development, and prosperity. Defense shouldn’t just mean missiles and jets but climate security, digital modernization, soft and hard infrastructure investments, and economic opportunities. In this regard, China has made inroads that are more aligned with ASEAN’s non-provocative needs.

Third, not all ASEAN countries view China as a threat: Cambodia, Laos, and Myanmar have close relations with China. East Timor, “the new kid” on the block, has good relations with China. Indonesia, Thailand, and Malaysia prefer equidistance. Vietnam and the Philippines are more assertive, particularly on the South China Sea (SCS) dispute. Still, even Vietnam won’t sign on to a U.S.-led containment agenda and will never compromise its thriving diplomatic and economic relations with China because that benefits Vietnam in every way. This fragmented outlook makes it nearly impossible for the U.S. to rally ASEAN as a unified bloc in defense. ASEAN unity on defense cannot be assumed; it must be delicately cultivated through regional mechanisms, not bilateral or multilateral coercion.

Fourth, China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), digital infrastructure investments, and trade integration through the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) have given it massive economic leverage across ASEAN. The U.S., by contrast, lacks a comprehensive economic strategy in Southeast Asia, especially after abandoning the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP). Without economic muscle, defense overtures look one-dimensional and opportunistic. You can’t build trust with missiles while ignoring markets.

Hence, the U.S. may find tactical partners in ASEAN, but winning the bloc’s strategic trust in defense matters is a tall order. Its current approach, steeped in deterrence, militarization, and bloc politics, clashes with ASEAN’s neutrality, balance, and quiet diplomacy DNA. To truly earn ASEAN’s trust, Washington must respect regional autonomy, prioritize non-military cooperation, address economic asymmetries, and speak less in terms of “us vs. them. ” Until then, the U.S. will remain a military partner of convenience, not a trusted security anchor in Southeast Asia.

PBBM SUSPENDS EDSA REHABILITATION FOR ONE MONTH AMID COMMUTER CONCERNS

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. on Sunday, June 1, ordered a one-month suspension of the planned major rehabilitation of EDSA to allow time for improved traffic mitigation measures and to lessen the burden on commuters.

Speaking during the launch of the Pamilya Pass 1+3 Promo at the MRT-3 GMA-Kamuning Station, Marcos said he was moved by concerns raised by commuters over the possible additional one to two hours of travel time during the two-year rehabilitation.

"Doon sa pinaplanong EDSA rehabilitation, ang daming bumalik na nag-aalala papaano 'yung trabaho namin? Eh kung ang pag-commute namin ay napakatagal na, madadagdagan pa ng isang oras, dalawang oras, wala na talaga, hindi na kami uuwi," Marcos said in Filipino.

The President directed Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) Secretary Manny Bonoan and Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) Chairman Vince Dizon to pause the rehabilitation project for one month, during which alternative solutions and new technologies will be considered.

EDSA, the 23.8-kilometer highway stretching from Pasay to Caloocan, already suffers from heavy daily traffic, which is expected to worsen once lane closures begin.

Marcos emphasized the need to strike a balance between long-term infrastructure improvements and short-term commuter welfare. "We will find a better way na hindi masyadong mahirap para sa ating mga commuter," he said.

A ‘massive’ road sinking near Phesama on National Highway 2—the viral road link between Kohima and Mao in Manipur—has prompted authorities to close the highway.
In a traffic advisory issued on Sunday, the deputy commissioner of Kohima informed that the sinking occurred between Chainage KM 192.050 and KM 192.150 on NH-2.
Effective immediately, all heavy vehicles en route to Kohima from Manipur have been directed to stop at Khuzama. Similarly, heavy vehicles travelling south towards Manipur from Dimapur will be stopped at Sechü-Subza.
